title: Restore My Sight
theme: Remaining faithful to God's truth without losing sight of His love for everyone.
opening: Can we become so concerned with protecting what we believe is right that we lose sight of the love we are called to share? Today's readings remind us that even when we believe we are following God faithfully, there may still be something we need Him to help us see.
prayer: Heavenly Father,  Help me remain faithful to Your truth without losing sight of Your love. When I become too certain of my own understanding, remind me that there may be something I have not yet seen. Give me the humility to listen, the wisdom to discern what is right, and the courage to act with compassion.  Lord Jesus, like the blind man who called out to You, I ask You to open my eyes. Help me recognize those I may overlook, listen to those I may not understand, and remember that every person is loved by You. May my desire to remain faithful never become an obstacle to sharing Your love.  Teach me to ask not only what is right, but how You want me to live what is right. Keep my faith rooted in love, and when I lose sight of that love, help me find my way back to You.  Amen.
body:
In today's first reading from Revelation, John receives a message from Jesus to the Church in Ephesus. Jesus acknowledges their hard work, perseverance, and refusal to tolerate evil. They have endured difficulties and remained faithful to His name. Yet He tells them, “You have lost the love you had at first.” He calls them to repent and return to their former works, warning that otherwise their lampstand will be removed.

I find this interesting because these people appear to be doing what is right. They are defending their faith, recognizing false teachings, and persevering through difficulties. So what have they lost? Perhaps they have grown weary, or perhaps they have become so involved in the responsibilities of protecting the Church that what began in love has gradually become more like business. They are still doing the work, but something about the love behind it has changed.

I cannot say that this is what happened, because the reading doesn't explain exactly how they lost their first love. But I wonder whether it reflects something we continue to struggle with in the Church today.

The Church has a responsibility to defend what is righteous and remain faithful to Christ's teachings. Yet those outside the Church, and sometimes those within it, may experience that defense as harsh or unloving. I think about the many situations in which we question the beliefs, choices, or lifestyles of others. Someone may be LGBTQ, divorced and remarried, practice yoga, have a Buddha statue in their garden, wear multiple piercings, or belong to another religion. These are very different circumstances, and not all of them are matters of moral disagreement. Yet how easily can we allow what we see, or what we think we understand, to shape our judgment of another person?

We want to love, but love itself requires examination. Loving someone does not necessarily mean agreeing with everything they do or believe. Yet defending what we believe is right does not give us permission to forget their dignity or the love God has for them. How do we remain faithful to the truth without allowing our defense of it to become more important than the people we are called to love?

Then we come to today's Gospel, and I wonder whether Jesus is showing us something about that very struggle.

As Jesus approaches Jericho, a blind man hears that He is passing by and begins calling out, “Jesus, Son of David, have pity on me!” The people around him rebuke him and tell him to be quiet, but he continues calling out even louder.

Jesus stops. Rather than allowing the crowd to silence the man, Jesus asks him, “What do you want me to do for you?” The man replies, “Lord, please let me see.” Jesus restores his sight, and the man follows Him, giving glory to God. When the people witness what has happened, they too begin praising God.

I find the connection between these readings remarkable. In Revelation, the Ephesians are faithful in their work, yet Jesus tells them something is missing. In the Gospel, a man who cannot see recognizes Jesus and calls out to Him, while those around him try to silence him. Jesus responds not by turning the man away, but by stopping and listening.

Perhaps this is something we need to remember when we become so caught up in protecting what we believe is right. Have we stopped to ask Jesus what He wants that protection to look like? Who should we be listening to? What should we say, when should we speak, and when should we simply listen? How do we recognize the difference between defending the truth and allowing our own perceptions to determine how we treat others?

God does not need us to protect Him. We are called to remain faithful to Him, but perhaps we need to ask more often how He wants that faithfulness expressed. We cannot assume that because our intentions are good, our understanding of a situation is always correct.

And perhaps that is why the blind man's request is so meaningful: “Lord, please let me see.”

We may believe we see clearly, especially when we are convinced we are doing what is right. But there may be something we have overlooked, someone we have failed to recognize, or a way of expressing our faith that needs to be reconsidered.

The Ephesians are called to recover their first love. The blind man asks to recover his sight. And the crowd, after witnessing Jesus' compassion, joins in praising God.

I don't think today's readings are asking us to abandon what we believe. I think they invite us to remember whom we believe in. Jesus is the one we are following, and perhaps before deciding how best to defend His teachings, we should ask Him to help us see what love requires.

Because ultimately, it is His love, not ours, that leads the way. And He loves everyone.
